title: Minibeasts
strapline: Six legs, eight legs, no legs at all — tiny creatures teaching gentle hands and big questions.
intent: Grow real respect for living things: minibeasts are the smallest creatures children can help, hurt or protect, and gentleness here becomes a habit for life.
Learn structure and classification through legs, wings and body parts — insects have six legs, spiders eight, worms none, and children can check.
Meet life cycles first-hand: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly is the best sequence story in nature.
Notice pattern and symmetry where nature puts it — ladybird spots, butterfly wings, spiral shells.
Connect small-world figures to the real minibeasts under our own logs and leaves outside.
implementation: Pair the figures with the real thing: a bug hotel, a wormery, or simply lifting a log together — always with 'gentle hands, and back where we found it'.
Model the anatomical vocabulary in passing — antennae, thorax, wing case — children collect these words like treasure.
Count legs out loud as a habit: 'one, two, three… six! So is it an insect?' — turning classification into a game with an answer children can find.
Tell the caterpillar's story with props in sequence, then leave the props out for children to retell and reorder.
Use magnifiers and pooters outdoors, and photograph finds so the small-world area holds a gallery of our own minibeasts.
Wonder rather than inform: 'I wonder why the worms were all under the wet log, not the dry one…'
Mirror-play with butterfly halves — paint one wing, fold, press — makes symmetry something children do, not just see.
key_questions: How could we work out whether this one is an insect?
Why do you think the worms like it under the log?
What will the caterpillar do next — and how do you know?
Where would be the kindest place to put this snail back?
Which minibeast would you be, and what would your day be like?

impact.text: Children handle real minibeasts with careful, gentle hands and return them where they were found — reminding friends to do the same.
Children count legs to classify their finds — six means insect, eight means spider — trusting the count as the answer.
Children notice and talk about the patterns and symmetry on butterfly wings and ladybird backs, and recreate them in paint and print.
Children tell the caterpillar-to-butterfly story in order and talk about the change happening inside the chrysalis.
Children hunt for minibeasts under logs and leaves on walks, collecting finds carefully and reporting back on where each one lived.
Children ask genuine minibeast questions — why do worms like the dark? where do butterflies sleep? — and expect proper answers.
Children sort the minibeast figures by their own criteria — wings and no wings, legs and no legs, ones that can sting.
Children use precise minibeast vocabulary in play — antennae, chrysalis, thorax, pollen — trying out new words as they meet them.

enhancements: A working bug hotel built with the children from bamboo, bricks and pinecones — checked weekly like a real hotel register.
A wormery or snail tank as a short-stay guest, with the children agreeing the care rules and the release day.
Magnifying pots, pooters and clipboards for a proper minibeast hunt survey of the garden.
Symmetry painting: fold-and-press butterfly wings, then match them to the real patterns in a field guide.
Playdough and pipe-cleaners for building anatomically correct insects — six legs, three body parts, count and check.
A life-cycle basket: eggs, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly props to sequence, muddle and re-tell.
Leaves with genuine caterpillar nibble-holes, collected on a walk, for close looking and drawing.

playing_exploring: Lifting a log is a genuine investigation — nobody, including the adult, knows what's under there.
Magnifiers turn familiar creatures strange and fascinating, inviting a second, longer look.
active_learning: Waiting for the chrysalis teaches the slowest, best lesson in patience the setting owns.
Children persist at the six-legged playdough insect until the count comes out right.
creating_thinking: Children form their own theories about where minibeasts live and test them log by log.
Linking the plastic figure, the photograph and the real creature under the leaf is classification thinking in action.
